newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain seen cutting rates but analysts mull details.
newsitem.headline: Spain seen cutting rates but analysts mull details.

text.p: The Bank of Spain is expected to sanction its seventh interest rate cut of the year before Christmas, but analysts are at odds over the amount and whether it will happen on Friday or on Christmas Eve.

A Reuter poll of 15 economists on Thursday showed that eight expected the central bank to cut its key money market rate at this week's regular repurchase tender, while seven said it would probably wait until at least the auction on December 24.
The Bank of Spain has cut its key money market rate six times this year, lowering it to the current rate of 6.75 percent from nine percent in early January.
While most economists agree that there is enough room for a seventh cut before year-end, they are split on the extent of the easing.
Of those in favour of a cut on Friday, half said the central bank would go for a 25 basis point cut while the other half said it would opt for a more meaty 50 basis points.
"The Bank of Spain has plenty of margin for easing and the market is currently discounting at least a 25 basis point cut on Friday," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
The steady decline in inflation to date would be one factor supporting a cut sooner rather than later, some economists said.
Others said the central bank would wait until it had November's data and the outcome of the Dublin summit in hand before taking the plunge.

"The Bank of Spain has room to lower rates tomorrow before the improvement in inflation for the whole year is revealed and before the November data which will probably register a low for 1996," said Juan Antonio Mielgo, economist at Bank of America, adding he expected a quarter percentage point cut on Friday.
November Consumer Price Index (CPI) data is also due to be released on Friday, just after the announcement of the results of the Bank of Spain's repurchase tender.
The CPI is forecast to rise 0.0-0.2 percent month-on-month for a 3.2 to 3.4 percent year-on-year increase, according to a Reuter survey of economists versus 3.5 percent in October.
The central bank will also have the intervention rate spread versus Germany in its basket of factors supporting a cut on Friday, some economists said.
With the German repurchase rate at 3.0 percent and Spain's key money market rate at 6.75 percent, economists pointed out that the spread would have to narrow to zero by 1999.
But others took a more prudent approach.
"Factors against a cut on Friday include the fact that the central bank does not know the outcome of the Dublin summit or the budget approval," said Urrutia.

EU leaders attending the Dublin summit are expected to reach a deal on a stability pact designed to ensure budgetary discipline continues after the start of European economic and monetary union (EMU) on January 1, 1999.
Economists said if the pact adopted adheres to the strict criteria demanded by Germany, this could put a negative slant on Spain's chances of entering EMU by 1999.
On the budget front, economists said the central bank may want to be reassured of its approval in the week of December 23.
The budget is expected to be safely passed by congress on the combined votes of the ruling Popular Party and its regional allies.
